title: Mermaid game for my wife - my workflow (what worked, what didn't)
author: Severe-Intern1705
selftext:
I'm a developer (not a game developer) - and my wife has been asking me to build her a mermaid game forever - she's actually a real life mermaid performer, and we take a lot of scuba shots.

Lately - I've started figuring out a workflow based on other people on this thread. What's worked for me has been:

\- Open AI for asset designs.  
Also - for this project - lots of real life pictures and scenes.  
\- Meshy for turnign those into 3d assets  
\- Blender for rigging, animations, particles  
\- Claude Code to orchestrate the whole thing.  
\- Godot as the engine

I've tried and had false starts with 9 versions of this game - earlier the models were just not good enough. Once Astra and Fable became a thing I was struggling to reproduce people's good results using Unity / Unreal. 

I had some good results with both Astra and Fable using threejs but very quickly got into performance problems and struggled with the aesthetic my wife had in mind. Unreal engine worked but even with the MCP I found the interactions were too slow vs three.js - making a scene change was taking forever.

So I settled with Godot as I figured models are better coding than they are with computer use.

The other two unlocks:  
\- Gave up on using Blender for my own assets - I always start with an existing design or use Meshy / (haven't tried Tripo). Maybe other people are having success and I'm doing something wrong but I found getting anything smooth and more realistic was just beyond what I could do within a 24h session with these models.  
  
I do still use Blender for rigging afterwards as I found Meshy at least to be really bad at it for non humanoid stuff.

Ultimately - despite me being a dev, I just did not touch code. I know enough to know where to run optimizations (for example the fish are GPU animations, and don't touch the CPU - and making some choices as to which animals are interactable and which ones are essentially just scene), what are the likely mistakes the model is doing, but so far a lot of this is purely vibe coded. I have not even opened the code base - I've stayed at the architecture layer at most.

**Open struggles:**  
  
1. I've got a pretty decent workflow for the animals, animations, and effects - the scene itself is still a bit hit or miss. Some of the more elaborate scenes I've been trying to work I've basically failed, even when I have good references.   
  
I think this is my ignorance on guiding the model on what should be textures vs new assets. Scene / world building is really something I'll need to improve.

  
2. Specific character animations - I've tried so many workflows here, even down to filming myself and making dots reference. The models I found really struggle to follow my instructions and / or I really struggle providing accurate isntrucitons for animations

The workflow that kind of worked for me has been using open ai to produce basically the key frames for the animation and then passing to claude as reference - but even then it's been a bit hit or miss.  


Thank you for reading - would love your feedback, and any suggestions!

comments.author: wakeofchaos
comments.body:
I’d say this is pretty friggin’ good for a solo dev with some ai tooling. I’m doing a couple games with a similar workflow but something I’ve accepted is that ai art and assets is just not worth bothering with. If you do the work of making the assets yourself, you can control the art style and the mesh detail, and make concessions where it’s needed for performance. 

For example, the seabed doesn’t need so much detail. There’s a way to make it interesting but still performant (think Subnautica. It’s less detailed than your game, but each object has a purpose. The sea floor is mostly flat, and there’s objects as assets, which is where you should lean). Like your level here is very beautiful, but you have to eventually make performance concessions. Things like less loading distance, or turning off the water effects at a certain distance can help

That said I think you’ve got a cool idea based on the amount of positive feedback here. I just think you’ve need an art direction and to maybe only use ai for code. It’s slower, but the end result is going to be significantly better imo because you’re avoiding that “ai art” look that so many games here have

replies.author: Severe-Intern1705
replies.body:
Yeah makes sense. What tools are you using for building your own assets ? My wife is the one with strong visuals of the two but she's struggling (her ways not mine) expressing her art through those tools.

We are considering lots of option ai enabled and none - of course there's basically 0 budget to hire proper 3d artists (or anything really hah) at this stage - that'd be the ideal solution

replies.author: wakeofchaos
replies.body:
Just straight blender. Having reference art is pretty helpful to get going, but I think you’ve can do a lot by just making things in blender from scratch. It’s gonna take forever but then you’ll know it was made well, hopefully and everything will have a specific look and feel. I think playing a bunch of indie games too can help, so you both can see what a few different approaches are to this side of things, then perhaps research how they got there. There’s a bunch of gdc talks on how this is done

Tbf I have seen some ai art games where the art isn’t as vital, but I’d wager that the look is gonna be a huge driver of interest in this game, so I think it’s worth trying to get it right, even if it takes a few more times and probably a few years

replies.author: Severe-Intern1705
replies.body:
Yeah I get you!

My idea right now is to get to a "good enough" stage and I'm sticking with "photorealis" as it's easier to create a cohesive art style there.

Once we release the demo we'll probably want to hire a few people to help us specifically on the art to be able to get a more polished look !

comments.author: alvaro_rami
comments.body: Could you elaborate on the animation workflow? Sounds promising and im struggling with the same, yours look really nice!

replies.author: Severe-Intern1705
replies.body:
For the animations I've used a combination of rigging and re-rigging the models until they looked well. Some models (like the jelly fish, and fish) - there were already available fabs with animations so I had claude re-rig new variants I've created with meshy onto the existing fabs (which will be credited)!  
  
For the mermaid where most of the attention was spent it was a painful combination of:  
1. Using 1 available rig I found [https://www.fab.com/listings/f56ef0ef-fc7f-44c3-8a72-601529c02bfb](https://www.fab.com/listings/f56ef0ef-fc7f-44c3-8a72-601529c02bfb)   
2. Using standard human rigging for the arms, heads, neck etc.  
3. Three custom workflows:

The custom workflow specifically was grabbing reference videos and having claude take keyframes to use for it's own reference for animating on Blender.  
A bit hit-or-miss it after a number of iterations it worked.

For the hand / arm movements I've really struggled, I've got TONS of videos of myself waving my arm like a fool trying to use the same approach to not avail. I've even build a custom tool that would get markers (like they use on movies) dotted onto my arms so the AI would have as reference.

The final part was using open AI image generation to create keyframes as well with markers.

NONE of the solutions worked 100% of the time, some of the animations took no less than 90 attempts of polishing them with Anthropic.

  
\_\_\_\_

One final part of my workflow that worked for me - as I still do have a full time job hah.

1. I purchased a 3rd party computer through DigitalOcean - I have my agent do most of the work there.  
2. I have my agent record demo videos of EVERYTHING - in particular I've had it build it's own specialized tool for demo-ing animations in blender an in game with all the different animation positions. Each of those becomes a video.  
So basically I prompt, get a video back and a way to easily evaluate the animation from various angles, say what I don't like - and prompt again.

  
I'm still refining this - and it's a PITA and is very innaccurate. It did not work at all for me with Astra or any other model than Opus 5.5 (well haven't tried with Fable). 

But I like the results and now I can just re-apply the animations to other things. Thankfully there's not THAT many types of new movements Ive introduced so far. Not looking forward to octopuses though lol

replies.author: Severe-Intern1705
replies.body:
Nice!

I'm still struggling with terrain tbh but  
  
The terrain also took a BUNCH of iterations. There's a lot of open materials / fab that I've started with - but I hated what the AI with Blender did with it.

I've tried giving it detailed direction which didn't work either. I think it's got the rocks and sand right, but the corals I still hated

Ultimately the current version I ended up:  
  
Having it take a reference video of a real life dive location that I'm using as loose reference - and with it:  
1. Build materials for the walls.  
2. Capture the texture.  
3. Isolate different models and build them into individual assets with Meshy for more interesting topologies.

The terrain workflow and animation workflow has been the two I've spent the most amount of time cracking my head against the wall with - and I'm still not loving the outcome - but it's come a LONG way.

Terrain and the character is the one thing that's been continously evolving through this project past iterations - so you could say this version of the terrain is probably iteration number 200+.

This one definetely not a one-shotted outcome, and I'm still trying to figure out a workflow that will give me more consistent results for building new terrain specifically and more interesting locations!
